items.title: "Delight in Solitude": Bodily Seclusion, Mental Calm, and the Path They Open

items.zh: 復次，如世尊言：汝等苾芻，當樂空閑，勤修觀行，內心安住正奢摩他者。謂能遠離臥具貪著，或處空閑，或坐樹下，繫念現前，乃至廣說。名樂空閑。當知此言顯身遠離。若能於內九種住心，如是名為內心安住正奢摩他。當知此言顯心遠離。
items.en: Furthermore, as the World-Honoured One said: "Monks, delight in solitude, diligently cultivate contemplation, and inwardly abide in right calm." "Delight in solitude" means being able to leave behind attachment to lodging and bedding, dwelling in an open place or sitting beneath a tree, with mindfulness present before one, and so on at length — this is called delighting in solitude. Know that this phrase shows bodily seclusion. "Inwardly abiding in right calm" means being able to settle the mind within by the nine ways of settling the mind. Know that this phrase shows mental seclusion.

items.zh: 若樂處空閑，便能引發內心安住正奢摩他。若內心安住正奢摩他，便能引發毘鉢舍那。若於毘鉢舍那善修習已，即能引發於諸法中如實覺了。
items.en: If one delights in dwelling in solitude, one can then draw forth the inward abiding in right calm. If one inwardly abides in right calm, one can then draw forth insight. If one has well cultivated insight, one can then draw forth a true and real realisation of things as they are among all phenomena.

items.title: Cultivating Concentration: The Immeasurable, the Constant-and-Thorough, and Right Mindfulness

items.zh: 復次，如世尊言：汝等苾芻，於三摩地當勤修習，無量、常委、安住正念者。謂先總標於三摩地勤修習已，後以三事別顯修相。無量者，謂四無量。常委者，謂常有所作，及委悉所作，故名常委。安住正念者，顯於四念住，安住其心。
items.en: Furthermore, as the World-Honoured One said: "Monks, towards concentration diligently cultivate the immeasurable, the constant-and-thorough, abiding in right mindfulness." Having first generally enjoined diligent cultivation of concentration, [the Buddha] then displays the marks of cultivation by three things. "The immeasurable" means the four immeasurables. "The constant-and-thorough" means constantly having something to do, and doing it thoroughly and completely — hence "constant-and-thorough." "Abiding in right mindfulness" shows settling the mind in the four foundations of mindfulness.

items.zh: 何故說此三種修相？謂依二種圓滿故。一者、世間圓滿，二者、出世圓滿。修無量故，便能引發世間圓滿。修正念故，便能引發出世圓滿。常委修故，於此二種速得通達；由此因緣，處二中說。是故但說三種修相。又無量者，顯奢摩他道。住正念者，顯毘
items.en: Why are these three marks of cultivation taught? Because of two kinds of completeness: worldly completeness and supramundane completeness. By cultivating the immeasurable, one draws forth worldly completeness; by cultivating right mindfulness, one draws forth supramundane completeness; and by the constant-and-thorough cultivation, one swiftly penetrates both — for which reason it is placed between the two. So only these three marks of cultivation are stated. Again, "the immeasurable" shows the path of calm; "abiding in right mindfulness" shows the path of insight.

items.title: Two Further Readings, and Why Calm Comes Before Insight

items.zh: 鉢舍那道。常委者，顯此二種速趣證道。又無量者，顯趣福德行。住正念者，顯趣涅槃行。常委者，顯趣二種速圓滿行。
items.en: This is stated in dependence on two kinds of completeness: worldly completeness and supramundane completeness. By cultivating the immeasurable, one draws forth worldly completeness; by cultivating right mindfulness, one draws forth supramundane completeness; by constant-and-thorough cultivation, one swiftly penetrates both. Again, "the immeasurable" shows the path of calm; "abiding in right mindfulness" shows the path of insight; "constant-and-thorough" shows these two swiftly advancing towards realisation. Again, "the immeasurable" shows conduct tending towards merit; "abiding in right mindfulness" shows conduct tending towards nirvāṇa; "constant-and-thorough" shows conduct swiftly perfecting both.

items.zh: 先於奢摩他善修習已，後與毘鉢舍那方得俱行。修此二種三摩地故，如實覺了所知境界。
items.en: Only after one has first thoroughly cultivated calm can it then run jointly with insight. By cultivating these two concentrations, one truly and really realises the objects to be known.

items.title: Skill in Absorption vs. Skill in Attainment: Four Kinds of Practitioner

items.zh: 復次，如世尊言：修靜慮者，或有等持善巧，非等至善巧。廣說如經嗢柁南頌。云何等持善巧？謂於空等三三摩地得善巧故。云何非等至善巧？謂於勝處、遍處、滅盡等至不善巧故。云何等至善巧，非等持善巧？謂於十種遍處等至及無想等至，若入若出俱得善巧，非於三三摩地。云何俱善巧？謂於彼二俱善巧故。云何俱不善巧？謂於彼二俱不善巧故。
items.en: Furthermore, as the World-Honoured One said: "Among those who cultivate dhyāna, some are skilled in the unifications but not skilled in the attainments," as the sūtra's summary verse explains at length. What is skill in the unifications? Being skilled in the three concentrations — emptiness and the rest. What is not being skilled in the attainments? Not being skilled in the masteries, the totalities, and the cessation-attainment. What is being skilled in the attainments but not in the unifications? Being skilled in entering and exiting the ten totality-attainments and the no-perception attainment, but not in the three concentrations. What is being skilled in both? Being skilled in both of these. What is being skilled in neither? Being skilled in neither of these.

items.zh: 如是於先所說等持、等至中，隨其所應，當善建立。
items.en: So too among all the unifications and attainments stated earlier, one should, as fitting, rightly establish this same fourfold analysis.

items.zh: 又說等持善巧非等至善巧者，謂於等持名句文身善知差別，非於能入等至諸行狀相差別。云何等至善巧非等持善巧？
items.en: Further, being skilled in concentration but not skilled in attainment means knowing well the distinctions of the names, phrases, and syllables of concentration, but not the distinctions in the features of the practices by which one enters the attainments. What is being skilled in attainment but not skilled in concentration?

items.title: Even a Bodhisattva Can Enter Countless Concentrations Without Knowing Their Names

items.zh: 謂如有一，善知能入隨一等至諸行狀相，亦能現入；而不善知此三摩地名句文身差別之相，亦不能知我已得入如是如是等持差別。有諸菩薩，雖能得入若百若千諸三摩地，而不了知彼三摩地名句文身，亦不能知我已得入如是如是等持差別。乃至未從諸佛所聞，及於已得第一究竟諸菩薩所而得聽聞，或自證得第一究竟。
items.en: Someone may well know the practice, state, and mark by which he can enter some given attainment, and can actually enter it — yet not well know the differentiating marks of that concentration's name and terms, nor be able to know "I have now entered such-and-such a unification." There are bodhisattvas who, though able to enter a hundred or a thousand concentrations, do not understand those concentrations' names and terms, nor can they know "I have now entered such-and-such a unification" — until they have heard this from the buddhas, or from bodhisattvas who have reached the ultimate stage, or have themselves realised that ultimate stage.

items.title: Abiding and Emerging: What Keeps a Concentration Stable, and the Three Reasons One Leaves It

items.zh: 云何為住？謂善取能入諸三摩地諸行狀相，善取彼故，隨其所欲能住於定，於三摩地無復退失。如是若住於定，若不退失，二俱名住。云何為出？謂如有一，於能入定諸行狀相不復思惟，於不定地分別體相所攝定地不同類法作意思惟，出三摩地。或隨所作因故，或定所作因故，或期所作因故，而出於定。
items.en: What is abiding? Well grasping the practice, state, and mark by which one enters the various concentrations — by grasping these well, one is able to abide in concentration as one wishes, with no further retrogression from it. Both abiding in concentration and not retrogressing from it are alike called "abiding." What is emerging? When one no longer attends to the practice, state, and mark by which one enters concentration, and instead attends to some object belonging to the unconcentrated ground, not of the same kind as the object of concentration, one emerges from concentration — whether from a cause one merely intends to act on, a cause one must act on, or a cause previously scheduled.

items.zh: 隨所作者，謂修治衣鉢等諸所作業。定所作者，謂飲食便利、承事師長等諸所作業。期所作者，謂如有一，先立期契，或許為他當有所作，或復為欲轉入餘定。由此因緣，出三摩地。
items.en: "What one intends to do" means tasks like mending one's robe or bowl. "What one must do" means tasks like eating, relieving oneself, or attending one's teacher. "What was previously scheduled" means someone who has set a prior arrangement — having promised to do something for another, or wishing to move into a different concentration. By these causes, one emerges from concentration.

blocks.text: Fascicle 13 completes the Stage of Meditative Absorption with a "gathering of essential scriptures": short sūtra phrases about meditation, each explained. Then, in rapid succession, it covers three more of the seventeen stages and opens the tenth. Today: solitude, the right attitude towards concentration, and the practical question of when and why one emerges from it.

"Delight in solitude" shows **bodily seclusion**; "inwardly abiding in right calm" shows **mental seclusion**, achieved through the nine ways of settling the mind. Venerable Miào Jìng on "leaving attachment to bedding": "It isn't that being very poor means freedom from attachment; if you cling to poverty, that's still clinging." Simplicity is not the same as non-attachment.

Right calm "draws forth insight". But Venerable Miào Jìng is careful: "It isn't that once I attain concentration it produces wisdom; no. If you don't separately study and reflect, concentration stays concentration." Day 93's point again: hearing and reflection must accompany meditation.

subs.head: The immeasurable, the constant, right mindfulness

blocks.text: The sūtra says to cultivate "the immeasurable, the constant-and-thorough, abiding in right mindfulness". The treatise: the immeasurable means the four immeasurables; constant-and-thorough means always having something to do and doing it thoroughly; right mindfulness keeps the mind on its object. Master Cháng Bǎi, citing the *Pīxún jì*: love, compassion, and joy wish beings worldly ease; equanimity turns towards the beyond.
Calm comes before insight in this sequence, as on Day 76.

subs.head: Skill in unification and in attainment

blocks.text: Some are skilled in the **unifications** (等持: the three concentrations of emptiness and the rest) but not in the **attainments** (等至: the masteries, totalities, and cessation), or the reverse, or both, or neither. Master Cháng Bǎi: unification extends even to scattered states, the last desire-realm concentration and threshold concentration; attainment requires a root absorption.

A bodhisattva may enter countless concentrations without knowing their names. Master Cháng Bǎi tells of Upagupta, who could not name the concentrations to his disciples and asked his own teacher, who replied that he did not know Upagupta's either. Experience precedes naming; names are for teaching.

What keeps a concentration stable is having mastered its marks. One emerges for three reasons: something one intends to do (mending a robe or bowl), something one must do (eating, the toilet, serving one's teacher), and something scheduled (a promised time). The treatise is practical: meditation fits into a life with duties.

Can one hear sounds in concentration? Master Cháng Bǎi: in the Mahāyāna view, ear-consciousness can momentarily hear in concentration, such as thunder; the *Vibhāṣā* says Maudgalyāyana heard elephants only after emerging. The question matters because it shows how Yogācāra understands concentration: the sense consciousnesses are quiet, not destroyed.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, what do "delight in solitude" and "inwardly abiding in right calm" each show?
options: delight in solitude shows bodily seclusion; abiding in right calm shows mental seclusion
quiz.why: "Know that this phrase shows bodily seclusion … being able to settle the mind within by the nine ways of settling the mind … Know that this phrase shows mental seclusion." Master Cháng Bǎi: amid noise and constant social obligations, calm and insight are impossible.

quiz.q: Does "leaving attachment to bedding" mean deliberately living in poverty, per Venerable Miào Jìng?
options: no — clinging to poverty is still clinging
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "It isn't that being very poor means freedom from attachment — if you cling to poverty, that's still clinging." Master Cháng Bǎi: bodily seclusion has degrees; without strong self-control, practice within the community.

quiz.q: The text says right calm "draws forth insight." Does wisdom then arise on its own, per Venerable Miào Jìng?
options: no — without separately cultivating wisdom, concentration stays concentration
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "It isn't that once I attain concentration it produces wisdom — no; if you don't separately study wisdom, concentration remains concentration, without insight." Master Cháng Bǎi: without concentration, scattered thinking is a candle in the wind.

quiz.q: The sūtra says to cultivate "the immeasurable, the constant-and-thorough, abiding in right mindfulness." How does the treatise explain them?
options: the immeasurable is the four immeasurables; constant-and-thorough is always acting and acting thoroughly; right mindfulness is settling the mind in the four foundations
quiz.why: "The immeasurable means the four immeasurables. The constant-and-thorough means constantly having something to do, and doing it thoroughly … Abiding in right mindfulness shows settling the mind in the four foundations of mindfulness." Venerable Miào Jìng: 委 means subtle and deep.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, what is being skilled in unifications but not attainments?
options: skilled in the three concentrations of emptiness and the rest, but not in the masteries, totalities, and cessation
quiz.why: "What is skill in the unifications? Being skilled in the three concentrations — emptiness and the rest. What is not being skilled in the attainments? Not being skilled in the masteries, the totalities, and the cessation-attainment." Venerable Miào Jìng: the three are wisdom practised in concentration.

quiz.q: Some bodhisattvas enter countless concentrations without knowing their names. What story of Upagupta does Master Cháng Bǎi tell?
options: unable to name the concentrations to teach his disciples, he called his teacher, who said, "You won't know mine, and I don't know my teacher's"
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "Upagupta didn't know the names of many concentrations and couldn't teach his disciples, so he invited his teacher"; "the teacher said: you won't know the concentration I enter, and I don't know my own teacher's." The reading note garbles the levels.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, for what three causes does one emerge from concentration?
options: an intended task (mending robe or bowl), a necessary task (eating, toilet, serving the teacher), a scheduled task (a prior promise or moving to another concentration)
quiz.why: "'What one intends to do' means tasks like mending one's robe or bowl. 'What one must do' means … eating, relieving oneself, or attending one's teacher. 'What was previously scheduled' means … a prior arrangement … or wishing to move into a different concentration." Master Cháng Bǎi: a scheduled talk at three o'clock.
